title: Abraham, Father of All Who Believe
summary: Paul turns to Abraham to show that justification by faith is not a new idea. Scripture says Abraham believed God and it was credited to him as righteousness, and David speaks of the blessing of forgiveness apart from works. Abraham was counted righteous before he was circumcised, so he is the father of uncircumcised and circumcised believers alike. His faith trusted the God who gives life to the dead, and the same words were written for those who believe in the God who raised Jesus.
story: In 3:21-31 Paul announced that God's righteousness is received through faith apart from works of the law, that boasting is excluded, and that God is the God of Gentiles too. He also claimed that the Law and the Prophets bear witness to this. Chapter 4 makes good on that claim by going back to the beginning of Israel's story, to Abraham in Genesis 12-22, the father of the Jewish people. If Abraham himself was put right with God by faith, then the gospel is not a break with Israel's Scriptures but the fulfillment of the promise God made to him: that in him all the families of the earth would be blessed (Genesis 12:3). Chapter 5 will build on this foundation with the words “since we have been justified through faith”.
historical:
Abraham was the great hero of Jewish faith, and in Paul's day he was often presented as a model of faithful obedience. The book of Sirach, written in the second century BC, praises him as one who kept the law of the Most High and was found faithful when tested. First Maccabees links the words of Genesis 15:6 to his faithfulness under trial, meaning the offering of Isaac. Later rabbinic tradition went further and held that Abraham kept the whole law before it was given. Paul's reading is deliberately different. He points out that Genesis 15:6, the verse about Abraham's faith being credited as righteousness, comes before the command of circumcision in Genesis 17 (more than thirteen years earlier, on Genesis's own timeline) and long before the law of Moses.

That chronology mattered to the Roman church. If Abraham was counted righteous while still uncircumcised, then Gentile believers did not need to become Jews to share in the promise, and Jewish believers could see their own father in the faith as the father of Gentiles too.
cultural:
Paul's argument uses the language of accounting. The verb credited (logizomai) appears eleven times in the chapter and was used of entering sums in a ledger. Verse 4 draws on the ordinary world of work: a laborer's wages are not a gift but something owed. Faith, by contrast, receives what is not owed. Paul's phrase in verse 5, that God justifies the wicked, would have startled a Jewish reader, since the law told judges never to acquit the guilty (Exodus 23:7, Proverbs 17:15).

Paul also uses a Jewish method of interpretation in which one passage is explained by another that shares a key word. Genesis 15:6 says righteousness was credited to Abraham; Psalm 32:1-2, attributed to David, speaks of the blessing of the one whose sin the Lord does not credit against him. The shared word lets Paul read the two together: being credited with righteousness means, at least in part, having one's sins forgiven.
literary: The chapter is a sustained reading of Genesis 15:6, which Paul quotes in verse 3 and returns to in verses 9, 22, and 23. It moves in four steps. First, faith rather than works (verses 1-8), supported by David's psalm. Second, faith before circumcision (verses 9-12), so Abraham is father of both groups. Third, promise rather than law (verses 13-17), because the law brings wrath while the promise rests on grace. Fourth, the character of Abraham's faith (verses 18-25), described as hope against hope in the God who gives life to the dead, and applied to believers who trust the God who raised Jesus. The chapter ends with a balanced, almost creedal line about Jesus: “He was delivered over to death for our trespasses and was raised to life for our justification.”

outline.t: Credited by faith, not earned by works
Before circumcision: father of all who believe
The promise comes by faith and rests on grace

doctrines.note: Abraham's faith was trust in God's promise when everything visible said it was impossible. Faith in Romans is not a work that earns, but reliance on the God who gives life to the dead and calls into being what does not exist.
God justifies the ungodly, crediting righteousness apart from works, and this includes the forgiveness of sins that David celebrates. Justification is a gift received, not wages paid.

The promise to Abraham, that he would be the father of many nations and heir of the world, is fulfilled as Jews and Gentiles share his faith. Circumcision was a sign and seal of a righteousness Abraham already had by faith.
Abraham in hope believed against hope. Christian hope rests on the same God who raised Jesus from the dead, so it is not wishful thinking but confidence in God's power and faithfulness.

words.note: Logizomai, to count, credit, or reckon. It appears eleven times in this chapter. It can mean recognizing what is already so, or reckoning to someone what is not theirs by right. Paul's contrast with wages in verse 4 shows the second sense: righteousness is credited as a gift. Debates about imputed righteousness in Reformation theology turn on this word.

Epangelia, promise. Paul sets the promise against the law: the promise came first and rests on God's word alone. The word links Abraham's story to the gospel, which Paul calls the fulfillment of what God promised beforehand (1:2).

Asebes, ungodly or wicked. Paul says God justifies the ungodly, a phrase that would shock anyone who knew the law's command not to acquit the guilty. The same word returns in 5:6: Christ died for the ungodly. That is how God can do it.

Sphragis, seal, the mark pressed into wax to certify a document or ownership. Paul calls circumcision a seal of the righteousness Abraham already had by faith. The sign confirmed the reality; it did not create it.

christ: The chapter's last verses make Abraham's faith and Christian faith the same kind of trust. Abraham believed God could bring life out of a body as good as dead and a barren womb; believers trust the God who brought Jesus back from the dead. Paul connects the two directly: the words it was credited to him were written for us also. Verse 25 sums up the gospel in two lines echoing Isaiah 53, where the servant is handed over for the sins of many: Jesus was delivered over for our trespasses and raised for our justification. His death deals with sin; his resurrection is God's vindication of him and of all who are joined to him. The promise that Abraham's offspring would bless the nations comes to its fulfillment in Christ.

hard.q: How does Romans 4 fit with James 2, which says Abraham was justified by works?
hard.a:
James writes that Abraham was justified by works when he offered Isaac (James 2:21-24), and he quotes the same verse Paul quotes, Genesis 15:6. On the surface the two seem to contradict each other.

Most interpreters, across traditions, conclude that they are answering different questions and using key words differently. Paul is asking how a sinner comes to be in the right with God, and he means by works the doing of the law as a basis for acceptance. James is confronting a faith that claims to believe but produces no action, and he uses justified to mean shown to be righteous. James's example is Abraham offering Isaac in Genesis 22, decades after Genesis 15:6; that act demonstrated the faith God had already credited. Paul himself insists that faith works through love (Galatians 5:6), and James insists that faith is at the root. Catholic, Orthodox, and Protestant traditions differ on how faith and works relate in justification, but all read these letters as complementary rather than contradictory.

questions: Paul contrasts wages with a gift. Where do you still think of your relationship with God as something you earn?
Abraham faced the facts about his age honestly and still trusted God's promise. What does it look like to trust God without pretending the facts are different?
Abraham is father of all who believe, whatever their background. How does that change how you see believers from other cultures or traditions?
